scenes.title: Post-quantum migration inventory
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains post-quantum migration inventory by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

The timeline shows protected traffic captured today, stored over years and potentially targeted by future cryptanalysis. This is the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk for sensitive long-lived information. The four inventory boxes identify TLS endpoints and key exchange, artifact and token signing, stored encrypted data and retention periods, and certificates or devices that are hard to upgrade. The risks differ for public-key algorithms and symmetric encryption, so prioritize data sensitivity and lifetime rather than assuming every algorithm fails identically.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Inventory cryptographic dependencies before choosing migration order and test client interoperability.

scenes.title: ML-KEM encapsulation
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains ml-kem encapsulation by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

Alice on the left owns an ML-KEM key pair with a public key that can be shared and a protected private key. Bob on the right uses Alice's public key to encapsulate, producing a ciphertext and his copy of a shared secret. He sends the ciphertext to Alice, who decapsulates it with her private key to derive the same secret. Both copies can then contribute to a secure protocol's key derivation. The banner distinguishes this mechanism from hybrid TLS using classical ECDH plus ML-KEM.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
ML-KEM establishes a shared secret; it is not a signature or a complete authenticated TLS protocol.

scenes.title: ML-DSA artifact signatures
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains ml-dsa artifact signatures by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

Start with the software publisher on the left creating an artifact, such as an installer or container. A protected ML-DSA private key signs the artifact; the artifact and signature travel to the verifier. The verifier uses the matching public key and expected publisher trust to check authenticity and integrity. The green checks mean the signature is valid and the content was not modified. The red warning emphasizes that signature verification does not encrypt the artifact, so its content may remain readable.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Plan compatible verifiers and transitional signing; a signature provides authenticity, not confidentiality.

scenes.title: Post-quantum crypto agility rollout
scenes.visual_overview: This slide explains post-quantum crypto agility rollout by following the pictured security architecture.
visual_walkthrough: Identify the featured AWS service and the full context

The four-stage path begins by inventorying TLS, certificates, signatures and key lifetimes. Next, pilot supported hybrid ECDH plus ML-KEM negotiation with selected clients. Then test across proxies, firewalls, load balancers and inspection systems, measuring the algorithms actually negotiated rather than relying on configuration. Finally, expand from canary rollout to wider deployment with monitoring, fallback rules and rollback. The lower lane handles ML-DSA artifact signatures separately, ensuring downstream tooling can verify them.
Distinguish permission, security and operational responsibilities
Cryptographic migration must preserve interoperability and availability while changing security algorithms.
